prompt:
[quiet, tired] Frank's booth. Just like the day guard said: the lamp, the cold tea, the jacket on the back of the chair. As if he'd stepped out for a minute.

[quiet, puzzled] In the jacket pocket, a pack of coarse salt, half empty. And a handful of loose salt. Why would a security guard carry salt?

[quiet, slow] Under the glass on the desk, a photo. Frank, an old man in work overalls, and a woman in a red dress. Her face was worn away, as if someone had stroked it with a finger a thousand times. On the back: 'Martha. Seventh floor. New Year's.'

[quiet, tired] In the drawer, Frank's phone, completely dead. I put it on the charger, in case the police want to know who he called.

The logbook was tied with string. On the cover, in Frank's hand: 'Before three. All of it.' I put it aside. Three was a long way off.

At ten my phone rang. An unknown number.

[quiet, serious] What really happened to Frank?

[curious] Why did you knock on the glass when you left?

[uneasy] 'It'? What's 'it'?

[casual] Is anyone else in the building?

[casual] Okay. See you in the morning.

[whispering, terrified] I knocked. Silence. Then, from inside — three knocks. Slow, heavy. As if someone were saving their strength.

[quiet, uneasy] Along the whole threshold, on the other side — a white line. Salt. Someone had poured it from the inside.

[calling out, nervous] Hey! Anyone in there?

[whispering, terrified] Not a sound. Only the light under the door flickered, as if someone had walked past the gap.

[quiet, tired] Probably the pipes. I kept telling myself that all the way upstairs.

[gentle] The woman in Frank's photo, in the red dress — is that Martha?

Did your wife work here too?

[quiet, serious] Did Frank say anything before he disappeared?

[careful] Who calls you?

[quiet, urgent] Gus. Whatever she says, don't answer. Promise me.

[quiet, warm] At a quarter past one, Lily called.

[warm] How's Biscuit?

[casual] You're at the dorm right now?

[hesitant] It's… weird here. The lights on the floors come on by themselves.

[warm] Go to sleep. You'll ace it.

[whispering, terrified] Frank's phone rang eleven times. Then a text came in: 'Frankie, son, come down to me. I'm downstairs.'

I hung up. My hands were shaking. Who calls an old man at two in the morning and asks him to come downstairs?

Hello?.. Someone on the line drew a breath. With relief. As if they had been waiting a long time.

[quiet, broken] He'd promised me. But it was Martha's voice.

[quiet, uneasy] So that was who called him downstairs. In the same voice that rang his phone tonight.

[quiet, slow] Salt. Like in his jacket pocket.

[quiet, realization] So that was who knocked back at me from behind the server room door at ten. It doesn't knock.

[gruff, trying to sound casual] It's the day guard. The agency gave me your number. So how's it going, new guy? Still alive?

[gruff, uneasy] I don't know. His last week he wasn't himself. Poured salt in the corners, by the doors, on the booth threshold. I figured it was for rats.

[low, serious] So you'd remember. Three knocks, that's me. I'll knock the same way in the morning. Frank used to say: it doesn't knock. It calls.

[gruff, a little too fast] I don't believe in those fairy tales. Neither should you. Sit tight till six, don't open the door for anyone, don't answer to your name. That's the whole job.

[gruff, softer] Gus, the cleaner. Mops the seventh floor, he's up there all night. Thirty years here. Go easy on him, he's a widower.

[low, serious] See you. Three knocks. Got it?

[warm, sad, old man] Martha. Our last New Year's. A month later she was gone. I've rubbed her face on that photo half away.

Martha. Bookkeeper, seventh floor, office seven-oh-seven. Thirty years we were here together. Now it's just me.

[old man, amused but uneasy] Kept asking if anyone calls me at night. I told him they do. He went white as a sheet. Poured salt in my pocket. Odd fellow.

[quiet, tender, old man] Martha. From seven, from seven-oh-seven. Don't think I'm crazy. I don't answer. I just come to listen.

[old man, moved, quiet] Thirty years she called me: to lunch, to come home… All right, son. I promise.

[warm, tired, teasing] You're up? Me too. Exam at eight tomorrow, and I'm sitting on the windowsill in the dorm and can't remember a thing.

[warm, laughing softly] Mom says he chases the delivery guys. He dragged your sweater into his doghouse and sleeps on it.

[teasing, warm] Where else? Two hundred miles from you, dummy. My roommate snores, so I'm out in the hallway.

[worried, serious] Don't scare me. Promise you'll call in the morning. First thing. And don't play the hero.

[warm, sleepy] Yeah. Love you, dummy. Good night.
